name: Garfinkle-Vachaspati Travelling Wave on a Cosmic String
description: A straight cosmic string carrying a wave of arbitrary shape that runs along it at the speed of light, together with the exact gravitational field of the wave. The geometry is a pp-wave whose transverse plane is the string's cone, curved wherever the wave passes while every scalar built from its curvature vanishes.
convention: The string's mass per unit length $\mu$ enters through $b = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: A cosmic string at rest is about as quiet as a gravitating object gets. Alexander Vilenkin's linearized calculation of 1981 has a straight string leave the space around it flat, with a wedge of angle $8\pi G\mu/c^2$ missing [vilenkin1981]. The exact solutions that J. Richard Gott and William Hiscock gave in 1985 agree: a cone, and no force on anything nearby [gott1985, hiscock1985]. So what happens when the string wiggles?¶The wiggles Tanmay Vachaspati chose to study in 1986 were the travelling waves: a wave of any shape running along the string in one direction at the speed of light [vachaspati1986, vachaspati1990]. Working in the weak field approximation, he found the metric around such a string [vachaspati1986]. The string now pulls: particles around it feel a force that falls off as $1/r$ [vachaspati1986]. The waves survive when the string is given its full thickness: two Vachaspatis, Tanmay and a coauthor who signs with the one name, showed in 1990 that travelling waves of arbitrary shape solve the field theory of a straight string, global or local [vachaspati1990].¶The exact answer came in 1990, when David Garfinkle found the metric of a travelling wave on a strongly gravitating string [garfinkle1990]. It is a pp-wave, one of the plane-fronted waves with parallel rays that Hans Brinkmann met in 1925 [garfinkle1990, brinkmann1925], and in the weak field limit it reduces to Vachaspati's [garfinkle1990]. In Garfinkle's coordinates the whole wave is one term in the metric, linear in the two directions across the string: $F = 2xA'' + 2yB''$, with $A$ and $B$ arbitrary functions of $ct - z$ [garfinkle1990, anderson1999]. In flat spacetime a term like that can be removed by a change of coordinates [anderson1999]. On the cone around a string it cannot, and the spacetime is curved [anderson1999].¶That September Garfinkle and Vachaspati gave the full solution together, the metric along with the scalar and gauge fields that make up the string [garfinklevachaspati1990]. They got it by applying a transformation to the solution for a long, straight, static string [garfinklevachaspati1990]. The transformation asks one thing of the solution it starts from: a family of light rays along which nothing changes, in technical terms a null Killing vector $k$ that is hypersurface orthogonal [kaloper1997]. The recipe is then a single line: add $F\,k_\mu k_\nu$ to the metric, with a weight fixed by $k$ itself, and leave the matter fields alone [kaloper1997]. The field equations still hold provided $F$ is constant along $k$ and solves Laplace's equation in the old geometry [kaloper1997]. Valeri Frolov and Garfinkle used the freedom in $F$ that December, putting a gravitational wave alongside the wave on the string and setting travelling waves on several parallel strings at once [frolovgarfinkle1990].¶Where is the string in all this? A change of coordinates puts it on show: in the new chart the string lies along $x = A(ct - z)$, $y = B(ct - z)$, a wiggle of arbitrary shape running up the string at the speed of light [anderson1999]. The wave keeps its shape and the metric is stationary, which Malcolm Anderson flagged in 1999, since a moving string is expected to radiate gravitational energy [anderson1999]. He traced the calm to the surface the string sweeps out in spacetime, its world sheet, which is intrinsically flat for every travelling wave [anderson1999].¶Curvature scalars are blind to the wave [kaloper1997]. That is a theorem of 1997, due to Nemanja Kaloper, Robert Myers, and Harold Roussel: every scalar invariant built from the curvature of the new metric equals the corresponding invariant of the old [kaloper1997]. Tidal forces do see it: on a black string carrying such a wave, they found, the tidal force on an infalling observer diverges at the horizon for every mode but the monopole [kaloper1997]. Light notices too: when Jaume Garriga and Patrick Peter sent a pulse of lightlike current along a superconducting string in 1994, they found a pp-wave with a deficit angle outside it, and the double image of a source behind the string shifted as the pulse went by [garriga1994].¶The transformation works just as well in the low energy limit of string theory, where Garfinkle used it in 1992 to set waves of any amplitude running along extremal black strings [garfinkle1992]. By 1996 it had reached the fundamental string itself: Atish Dabholkar, Jerome Gauntlett, Jeffrey Harvey, and Daniel Waldram built the oscillating strings of the perturbative spectrum as exact supergravity solutions, and singled out the term linear in the transverse coordinates as the one that matches onto an oscillating string source [dabholkar1996]. When Gary Horowitz and Donald Marolf counted the states of black strings carrying travelling waves, in 1997, the count matched the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy [horowitz1997]. They called the solutions "quite remarkable in that the waves propagate indefinitely without radiating to infinity or falling into the horizon" [horowitz1997]. A string wound many times around a circle and carrying a travelling wave was the starting point, in 2001, of Oleg Lunin and Samir Mathur, who mapped its solution by dualities onto the D1-D5 system [lunin2001].

related.text: The string with its wave switched off. With $A = B = 0$ only the cone is left [garfinklevachaspati1990].
The string's mass switched off. At $b = 1$ the cone opens into a plane and the metric is a pp-wave in Brinkmann's form [garfinkle1990].
The string taken away. At $b = 1$ the travelling wave's profile is linear in $x$ and $y$, and a change of coordinates removes it [anderson1999].
Another pp-wave whose profile is harmonic off a line, there the logarithm around a massless particle and here the dipole around a string [aichelburg1971, dabholkar1996].
A straight string given spin where this one is given a wave. Both leave every curvature scalar at zero [deser1992time, kaloper1997].

coordinates.name: Null Conical

parameters.description: $b = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$, with $\mu$ the string's mass per unit length, $0 < b \le 1$; the deficit angle is $2\pi(1 - b)$

Wave profile, a dimensionless function of $u$, $r$, and $\phi$. The metric is a vacuum solution where $F$ solves Laplace's equation on the cone, $\partial_r^2F + \partial_rF/r + \partial_\phi^2F/(b^2r^2) = 0$, and the string's own travelling wave is $F = -2\ell(br/\ell)^{1/b}(A''\cos\phi + B''\sin\phi)$

coordinates.convention: We use the null coordinates $u = ct - z$ and $v = ct + z$, both lengths, with $r$ the proper distance from the string and $\phi$ the angle about it, periodic in $2\pi$. We leave the profile $F$ free, so no component assumes a field equation. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Isotropic

parameters.description: $b = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$, with $\mu$ the string's mass per unit length, $0 < b \le 1$; the deficit angle is $2\pi(1 - b)$
An arbitrary length; changing it rescales $x$ and $y$, which is a change of coordinates
Displacement of the string along the first transverse direction, a length and an arbitrary function of $u$
Displacement of the string along the second transverse direction, a length and an arbitrary function of $u$
Coordinate distance from the string; the proper distance is $r = (\ell/b)(\rho/\ell)^b$

coordinates.convention: We use the null coordinates $u = ct - z$ and $v = ct + z$, both lengths, with Garfinkle's isotropic coordinates $x$ and $y$ across the string, which lies along $x = y = 0$. A prime is a derivative with respect to $u$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Moving String

parameters.description: $b = 1 - 4G\mu/c^2$, with $\mu$ the string's mass per unit length, $0 < b \le 1$; the deficit angle is $2\pi(1 - b)$
An arbitrary length; changing it rescales $x$ and $y$, which is a change of coordinates
Displacement of the string along the first transverse direction, a length and an arbitrary function of $u$
Displacement of the string along the second transverse direction, a length and an arbitrary function of $u$
Coordinate distance from the string at fixed $u$; the proper distance is $(\ell/b)(\rho/\ell)^b$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, V, X, Y)$ in which the string lies along $X = A(u)$, $Y = B(u)$: $X = x + A$, $Y = y + B$, and $V = v + 2xA' + 2yB' + \int(A'^2 + B'^2)\,du$, with $v$, $x$, and $y$ those of the isotropic chart. A prime is a derivative with respect to $u = ct - z$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
geodesics: \ddot{V} - \left(2\left(1 - \left(\dfrac{\rho}{\ell}\right)^{2 - 2b}\right)\left(A'\,A'' + B'\,B''\right) - \dfrac{2\left(b - 1\right)\left(\left(A'\right)^2 + \left(B'\right)^2\right)\left(\left(X - A\right)A' + \left(Y - B\right)B'\right)}{\rho^2}\right)\dot{u}^2 - \dfrac{4\left(b - 1\right)\left(\left(A'\right)^2 + \left(B'\right)^2\right)\left(X - A\right)}{\rho^2}\dot{u}\dot{X} - \dfrac{4\left(b - 1\right)\left(\left(A'\right)^2 + \left(B'\right)^2\right)\left(Y - B\right)}{\rho^2}\dot{u}\dot{Y} + \dfrac{2\left(b - 1\right)\left(\left(X - A\right)A' - \left(Y - B\right)B'\right)}{\rho^2}\dot{X}^2 + \dfrac{4\left(b - 1\right)\left(\left(X - A\right)B' + \left(Y - B\right)A'\right)}{\rho^2}\dot{X}\dot{Y} - \dfrac{2\left(b - 1\right)\left(\left(X - A\right)A' - \left(Y - B\right)B'\right)}{\rho^2}\dot{Y}^2 = 0

\ddot{X} - \left(\left(1 - \left(\dfrac{\rho}{\ell}\right)^{2 - 2b}\right)A'' - \dfrac{\left(b - 1\right)\left(\left(X - A\right)\left(A'\right)^2 - \left(X - A\right)\left(B'\right)^2 + 2\left(Y - B\right)A'\,B'\right)}{\rho^2}\right)\dot{u}^2 - \dfrac{2\left(b - 1\right)\left(\left(X - A\right)A' + \left(Y - B\right)B'\right)}{\rho^2}\dot{u}\dot{X} + \dfrac{2\left(b - 1\right)\left(\left(X - A\right)B' - \left(Y - B\right)A'\right)}{\rho^2}\dot{u}\dot{Y} + \dfrac{\left(b - 1\right)\left(X - A\right)}{\rho^2}\dot{X}^2 + \dfrac{2\left(b - 1\right)\left(Y - B\right)}{\rho^2}\dot{X}\dot{Y} + \dfrac{\left(1 - b\right)\left(X - A\right)}{\rho^2}\dot{Y}^2 = 0

\ddot{Y} - \left(\left(1 - \left(\dfrac{\rho}{\ell}\right)^{2 - 2b}\right)B'' - \dfrac{\left(b - 1\right)\left(2\left(X - A\right)A'\,B' - \left(Y - B\right)\left(A'\right)^2 + \left(Y - B\right)\left(B'\right)^2\right)}{\rho^2}\right)\dot{u}^2 - \dfrac{2\left(b - 1\right)\left(\left(X - A\right)B' - \left(Y - B\right)A'\right)}{\rho^2}\dot{u}\dot{X} - \dfrac{2\left(b - 1\right)\left(\left(X - A\right)A' + \left(Y - B\right)B'\right)}{\rho^2}\dot{u}\dot{Y} + \dfrac{\left(1 - b\right)\left(Y - B\right)}{\rho^2}\dot{X}^2 + \dfrac{2\left(b - 1\right)\left(X - A\right)}{\rho^2}\dot{X}\dot{Y} + \dfrac{\left(b - 1\right)\left(Y - B\right)}{\rho^2}\dot{Y}^2 = 0
